title: How To Handle A Student Who Talks Back
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lays out a five-step sequence for responding to a student who talks back after receiving a warning: turn away rather than confront, ignore the outburst for the moment, wait roughly ten minutes to let the student reflect, then enforce the next consequence and walk away without discussion, and finally contact parents -- framed as a right-to-know notification rather than an added punishment. His reasoning is rooted in the same theme running through much of his writing: emotional confrontation in the moment either shows anger the teacher will regret or lets the student off the hook by turning it into a negotiation, whereas letting the student sit with the moment prompts genuine reflection and regret. He's explicit that this strategy applies equally at the elementary and high school level, calling it more important now than ever, and closes by emphasizing that showing no emotional reaction and refusing to justify or discuss the disrespect is what makes the consequence land as a real lesson rather than something the student can talk their way out of.
points: Follow a five-step sequence after a talk-back: turn away, ignore for now, wait roughly ten minutes, enforce the next consequence and walk away, then contact parents.
Waiting before responding lets the student's own reflection and regret do the work that a direct confrontation would undercut.
Show no emotional reaction to disrespect -- reacting emotionally either signals anger the teacher will regret or turns the moment into something the student can argue their way out of.
This approach is presented as equally applicable at elementary and high school levels, not just for younger students.
quotes: Not much fires a teacher up more than a student talking back. It has a special way of getting under the skin because . . .
If you stand there and eyeball the student, then you’re either going to show how angry it makes you or say something you’ll regret.
Allow the student to consider they made a mistake. When you don’t respond right away, it prompts reflection and often regret. Wait at least ten minutes.
Brazen disrespect must be reported to parents—not so much as an added consequence but because parents have a right to know.
Resist the urge to pull the student aside for a talking-to, lecture, or the like. Have no discussion whatsoever. Allow your classroom management plan to do its job without your interference.
I recommend this strategy for elementary students as well as high school . Yes, at the most challenging schools. Yes, in this day and age. In fact, it’s more important now than ever before.
